newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: James Packer says media rules should change.
newsitem.headline: James Packer says media rules should change.

text.p: James Packer, the son of billionaire businessman Kerry Packer and the managing director of the family's Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd, said on Friday Australian media rules should not continue to prevent the company from bidding for newspaper publisher, John Fairfax Holdings Ltd.
"Why shouldn't we be allowed to buy Fairfax, an Australian newspaper company, and grow our business?," he said in an interview on the Nine Network's A Current Affair programme.

Kerry Packer has met Australian Prime Minister John Howard in recent weeks to discuss the government's planned changes to national media rules which currently prevent ownership of television stations and newspapers in key cities.
Publishing and Broadcasting owns the top-ranked Nine Network and also has 15 percent of Fairfax, the maximum allowed under the current cross-media rules.
The government is expected to announce changes to the rules in the next two weeks.

James Packer said a Fairfax takeover would create a major Australian media company with export potential and would be in contrast to the tendency of foreign ownership now evident in local media -- a reference to News Corp Ltd whose operations account for about 70 percent of capital city newspaper circulation.
Although born in Australia, News Corp executive chairman Rupert Murdoch is now a U.S. citizen, a prerequisite for his gaining ownership of the Fox television division.
"Ninety percent of Australian newspapers are controlled by foreigners," he said.

"Why as an Australian company, an Australian media company - which prevents us from expanding our business internationally .... we can't buy television stations in England, we can't buy television stations in America - why shouldn't we be allowed to buy Fairfax?"

The Sydney Morning Herald, which is owned by Fairfax, said on Friday that the government favoured changing media ownership laws to allow Packer to buy Fairfax, provided he sold the group's national financial daily, The Australian Financial Review.
Fairfax also owns the Melbourne Age daily and magazines.
Executives from British publisher Pearson Plc and its half-owned The Economist magazine met with Australian government officials this week to discuss the planned media rule changes.
Some Fairfax papers and The Australian newspaper have variously reported this week that Pearson was keen on acquiring The Australian Financial Review.
Packer is the second largest shareholder in Fairfax behind Brierley Investments Ltd of New Zealand, which has 20 percent and which under foreign investment media rules cannot go beyond 25 percent.
Fairfax shares ended five cents higher on Friday at A$3.24, valuing the publisher at A$2.46 billion based on its 758.76 million shares on issue.

Media analysts expect Packer to launch a scrip based bid which would value Fairfax at about A$3.50 per share, but some have recently said this price could prove too rich for Packer despite his passion for taking control of the historic group.
